the effect of heterogeneous intratumoral activity distributions on the absorbed dose distribution in the treatment of solid tumors by radionuclide delivery.
the influence of a nonuniform intracellular activity distribution on the absorbed dose distribution in solid tumors.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a heterogeneous intratumoral distribution of activity is detrimental to radionuclide treatment of solid tumors.
the absorbed dose delivered to the center of the tumor is a strong function of the tumor's radius, and the absorbed dose to the normal tissue is a function of tumor radius and radionuclide energy.
the absorbed dose to the center of the tumor is dependent on the radionuclide used and the tumor diameter.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the absorbed dose to the center of tumors with diameters of 1,3,5,10, and 10 mm is 0.7, 2.5, 3.6, 4.8, and 4.5 Gy, respectively.
the radionuclids 131I and 90Y are the most effective in the treatment of small tumors, while the radionuclide 188Re is most effective in the larger tumors.
the absorbed dose delivered to the tumor center is dependent on tumor diameter, intratumoral activity concentration, and radionuclide half-life.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a heterogeneous intratumoral activity is a significant problem for the treatment of solid tumors.
the use of radionuclidies with higher beta energy is a better option for radionuclide treatment of solid tumors.
radionuclide treatment is more effective in tumors with diameters between 3 and about 15 mm in size.
